topic.en: Three texts: what archaeologists learn from rubbish, why so many cities are built on a grid, and the argument about whether children should first be taught in their home language.

textTitles: Why so many cities are built on a grid
Should children first be taught in their home language?

paragraphs.text: Archaeologists spend much of their working lives digging through other people’s rubbish. The palaces and temples that appear in guidebooks are exceptions; the ordinary material of the past is broken pottery, animal bones, discarded tools, ash from fires and the shells of eaten shellfish, and most of it survives because someone threw it away. Much of it was never meant to be seen again. Heaps of such waste, known as middens, can accumulate over centuries beside settlements, and because they build up layer by layer, with the oldest material at the bottom, they offer a record of daily life that is often more complete and more honest than anything written down at the time.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Honesty is the key point. Written sources record what people wished to be remembered, or what officials needed to know, and they were produced overwhelmingly by the literate and the powerful. Rubbish is indifferent to status. A household that claimed in public to live frugally, or a town that boasted of its prosperity, left in its middens the evidence of what it actually ate, bought and wasted. For many societies that left no writing at all, discarded material is the only record there is, and even for literate societies it reveals the lives of the majority who never wrote anything down.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Some of the largest middens are made almost entirely of shells. Along coasts in many parts of the world, communities that gathered shellfish left mounds that could be several hundred metres long and many metres high. Analysing the size of the shells in successive layers allows researchers to see whether people were harvesting more than the shellfish population could replace: when shells become steadily smaller over time, it usually means that the larger, older animals were being collected faster than they could grow. Some mounds show such declines followed by a recovery, suggesting that communities moved away or changed their practices before stocks collapsed. Shell mounds are also valuable because the shell reduces the acidity of the soil, which helps bones and other remains to survive.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Animal bones tell a different story. The species present, the age at which the animals were killed and the marks left by butchery tools reveal whether people hunted or kept livestock, which parts of an animal were valued and how meat was shared. Cut marks can even show whether bones were split to extract marrow, often a sign of scarcity. In towns, the bones from wealthy households often come from younger animals and better cuts than those from poorer districts. Plant remains, which survive when they are burned or waterlogged, add further detail: seeds, grains and fragments of imported fruit can show what was grown locally and what was brought from far away.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The method has also been applied to the present. In the 1970s, a research project in a North American city began collecting and sorting the rubbish of selected households and comparing it with what the same households said about their habits in interviews. The differences were striking. People consistently reported eating more fruit and vegetables and drinking less alcohol than their bins suggested, and they tended to underestimate how much food they threw away. The project’s founders argued that studying modern waste could correct the distortions of surveys, much as archaeology corrects those of ancient texts. Critics noted that households which knew they were being studied might change what they threw away.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Rubbish can mislead, however. What survives depends on what was thrown away, where it was thrown and in what conditions it lay. Metal was often too valuable to discard and was melted down for reuse, so its scarcity in a midden does not mean that it was rare. Organic material decays unless it is burned, frozen, dried or sealed in waterlogged ground. Some communities burned their waste or carried it out to sea, leaving little behind. Archaeologists therefore have to reconstruct not only what people used but also how they got rid of it before they can interpret what remains.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Dating the layers is another challenge. Because middens accumulate gradually, archaeologists can usually establish the order in which material was deposited, but not always how long each layer took to form. Objects that can be dated independently, such as coins, pottery of a known style or charcoal suitable for radiocarbon analysis, act as markers. Burrowing animals, later digging and the collapse of heaps can mix layers together, however, so that a fragment found near the bottom is not necessarily older than one found above it. Careful excavation therefore records the exact position of every find, so that such disturbances can be recognised later.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Modern landfills will one day become the middens of the future, and they will be larger than anything the past produced. Some are already being mined for metals and other materials that were thrown away when they were cheap. Because they are sealed and compacted, material in them breaks down far more slowly than many people assume: excavations of landfill sites have recovered newspapers that were still readable decades after they were buried. Future archaeologists may find our rubbish easier to read than our digital records, which depend on machines and formats that may not survive. It is an uncomfortable thought that the most durable account of our lives may be the one we tried hardest to hide.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Why so many cities are built on a grid

paragraphs.text: Seen from the air, many cities are made of rectangles. Streets cross one another at right angles, blocks are of similar size, and the pattern runs on, sometimes for many kilometres, with little regard for hills or rivers. In some places it seems to have been drawn with a ruler across the landscape, and in a sense it was. The grid is often thought of as a modern, particularly American, invention, but it is one of the oldest forms of planned settlement. Towns laid out in regular blocks existed in the Indus valley more than four thousand years ago, and planned grids appear in ancient China, Egypt and Greece. Wherever authorities have founded a town from nothing, rather than letting it grow, they have been drawn to the straight line.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The reasons are partly practical. A grid is easy to survey: once a starting point and a direction are fixed, the whole plan can be marked out with little more than ropes and measuring rods, and it can be extended in any direction as the population grows. It divides land into plots of equal size that can be sold, taxed or allocated without dispute. The Romans laid out new military camps and colonies to a standard plan with two main streets crossing at the centre, so that soldiers arriving at any camp in the empire would know where to find everything. Many Greek colonies around the Mediterranean had been laid out in much the same way.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The grid has also had a political meaning. Colonial powers used it to impose order on newly acquired territory, and many cities founded by Spain in the Americas followed royal instructions issued in the sixteenth century, which specified a central square, straight streets and the positions of the main public buildings. In the United States, a national survey from the late eighteenth century divided much of the interior into square-mile sections, so that the grid extended beyond the cities into the countryside itself, and farms, roads and county boundaries still follow its lines. From the window of an aeroplane, the pattern is still visible across thousands of kilometres of farmland.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Critics have long complained that the grid is monotonous and indifferent to landscape. Streets laid out on paper in a distant office may climb hills too steep for comfortable walking or cut through valleys that would have been better left alone, and the uniform blocks can make it hard to find one’s way, since every junction looks much like every other. Some visitors find grid cities disorienting precisely because they are so regular. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, planners in several countries turned against the grid in favour of curving streets and cul-de-sacs, which they believed would create quieter, more attractive residential areas that followed the natural contours of the land.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Defenders of the grid reply that it makes directions easier, not harder. In many grid cities streets are numbered or named in sequence, so that an address indicates roughly where a building lies, and visitors can work out how far they must walk by counting blocks. Some cities combine the grid with a few diagonal avenues that cut across it, providing faster routes between important points and creating open squares and triangular plots where they meet. Such diagonals were a favourite device of planners who wanted grand views towards monuments or public buildings, and several capital cities owe their character to them.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The curving layouts that replaced the grid are now themselves being reconsidered. Suburbs built around curving roads and dead ends are often pleasant for residents but difficult to cross on foot, because the path between two nearby points may require a long detour to the nearest main road. Transport researchers have found that people living in such areas walk less and drive more than those living in grids of similar density, partly because the grid offers many alternative routes between any two points. Traffic in a grid can spread across parallel streets, whereas in a branching network it is funnelled onto a few busy main roads. Emergency services also reach addresses more quickly when there are several ways in.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The size of the blocks matters as much as the pattern. Some grids have very large blocks, which leave long distances between junctions and encourage fast traffic, while others have small blocks of sixty or eighty metres, which make walking easy and slow vehicles down. Several historic city centres that are admired for their liveliness have grids with small blocks and narrow streets, and planners designing new districts increasingly aim for a similar scale rather than for the wide avenues favoured in the middle of the twentieth century. Smaller blocks also mean more street corners, and corners are where shops and cafés tend to gather.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Few planners today argue for a pure grid or a pure network of curves. More common is a flexible pattern that keeps the connectivity of the grid while bending it to fit the landscape, preserving views and allowing some streets to be quieter than others. The oldest lesson of the grid may simply be that the shape of a city’s streets has consequences that last far longer than the people who drew them. A plan marked out with ropes and rods can govern how people move for thousands of years.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Should children first be taught in their home language?

paragraphs.text: Around the world, hundreds of millions of children begin school in a language they do not speak at home. In some countries this is because the language of education is a national or former colonial language; in others it is because families have migrated, or because the local language has no tradition of being written. Governments often assume that the sooner children are immersed in the dominant language, the better their prospects will be. A growing body of research suggests that this assumption may be mistaken, and that children learn more, including more of the dominant language, when they start in the language they already know. The question matters for education in almost every part of the world.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The argument rests on how reading develops. Learning to read involves connecting written symbols to words whose sounds and meanings the child already knows. A child who is taught to read in an unfamiliar language must learn the code and the language at the same time, and many fall behind in both. The difficulty is less obvious to adults, who learned to read long ago and in a language they already spoke. The linguist Anna Petrova, who has compared schools in several multilingual countries, found that children who learned to read first in their home language were reading more fluently in the national language by their fifth year than children who had been taught in it from the start. The gap was widest among children whose families had few books at home.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Supporters of early immersion reply that such findings depend heavily on the quality of the teaching, and they have a point. The economist Marcus Webb argues that home-language programmes are often introduced without enough trained teachers or printed materials, and that a poorly resourced programme in the home language may do more harm than a well-resourced one in the national language. In his view, the language of instruction matters less than whether children have books, qualified teachers and manageable class sizes. He also points out that many families see the national language as the key to employment.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: I accept that resources matter, but I think Webb underestimates how much language itself affects what happens in a classroom. A teacher speaking to children who understand little of what is said cannot easily check their understanding, and lessons often fall back on repetition and copying. The anthropologist Grace Mbeki, who spent two years observing primary classrooms, describes pupils chanting sentences they could not translate and teachers switching into the home language informally to explain anything difficult, while official policy pretended that this was not happening. Such classes may look orderly, she notes, while very little is being learned.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: A further concern is what happens to the home language itself. Children who are taught that their family’s language has no place in school may come to regard it as inferior, and some stop using it altogether, becoming reluctant to speak it even with their grandparents. Petrova points out that this loss has consequences beyond sentiment: children who keep developing their first language tend to find it easier to learn additional languages later, because they transfer skills such as reading strategies from one language to another. Abandoning the home language, she argues, weakens the foundation on which the second is built. Her view is shared by many linguists, though not by all.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The strongest evidence comes from countries that have tried both approaches. Where well-planned home-language programmes have been introduced across whole regions, with textbooks written in local languages and teachers trained to use them, reading results in the early years have generally improved, and the proportion of children leaving school early has often fallen. The improvements are not automatic, and several programmes have produced little benefit because the switch to the national language came too abruptly, often after only two or three years. Researchers now tend to recommend a longer period of gradual transition, with both languages used side by side.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The practical difficulties should not be dismissed. In cities where dozens of languages are spoken, it may be impossible to offer teaching in all of them, and written materials may simply not exist for languages with no written tradition, and training teachers for each language takes years. The historian Leon Duval notes that several countries which introduced home-language education on a large scale later abandoned it, not because it failed in the classroom but because parents, anxious for their children to succeed in the national language, demanded that it be taught from the first day. Their fears, in other words, shaped policy more than the evidence did.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: My own view is that the evidence favours starting in the home language wherever it is realistic to do so, which will not be everywhere, with the national language introduced gradually and taught well. Parents’ fears are understandable, but they rest on a misunderstanding: the aim of teaching first in the home language is not to keep children away from the national language but to give them a firmer path towards it. Where resources make this impossible, schools should at least allow teachers to use the home language to explain, rather than forbidding what many of them already do.
paragraphs.label: H
